title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether middle-school students can productively regulate inquiry when using ChatGPT for learning. The core problem is not literacy instruction but students’ ability to initiate, evaluate, and regulate question-asking cycles with generative AI during school tasks. The authors investigate whether students can distinguish effective from ineffective prompts, judge the usefulness of AI responses, ask follow-up questions when needed, and ultimately reach accurate conceptual understanding. They also test how these behaviors relate to metacognition, prior knowledge, and attitudes toward AI.

The study used six science investigation tasks in which students interacted with ChatGPT 3.5 during a one-hour school session. For each task, students saw either an efficient or inefficient suggested prompt, judged that prompt’s quality, optionally used it or wrote their own, evaluated every AI response they received, and then wrote a short answer in their own words. Researchers analyzed prompt discrimination, answer-evaluation sensitivity, follow-up behavior, and final task success, while also collecting questionnaire data on AI attitudes and metacognitive competencies.

Participants were 63 French students aged 14–15 from four middle-school institutions in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region. The study took place during normal school hours with laptops provided by the research team, while task materials were given on paper. This was an observational study rather than a controlled intervention trial: although prompt suggestions were randomized at the task level, the paper primarily analyzes students’ naturally occurring behaviors, individual differences, and associations with performance rather than treatment effects between groups.

The main conclusion is that students showed substantial over-reliance on ChatGPT and weak metacognitive regulation. On average, they were near chance in distinguishing efficient from inefficient prompts and informative from uninformative AI answers, seldom asked follow-up questions, and achieved only moderate task success despite unrestricted AI access. More positive attitudes toward AI were associated with poorer judgment of prompt and answer quality, whereas metacognitive regulation was associated with better prompt discrimination. The authors argue that AI literacy instruction should move beyond technical familiarity toward explicit training in metacognitive regulation, epistemic vigilance, and strategically effortful use of generative AI.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical K-12 study with clear methods and quantitative analyses, but it is a small single-group observational/correlational design without a control group or random assignment to intervention versus non-intervention conditions. As a preprint, it also has some peer-review uncertainty and does not meet stronger causal credibility standards.
impact_tier_rationale: Observed outcomes are predominantly negative: students showed chance-level discrimination of prompt and answer quality, very limited follow-up regulation, and only moderate science-task success despite AI access. The paper does not report positive literacy or academic effect sizes, and the main implication is risk of over-reliance rather than demonstrated benefit.

interventions.use_case: Middle-school students used ChatGPT 3.5 as an unrestricted conversational inquiry partner during science investigation tasks, with researchers analyzing prompt quality judgments, evaluation of AI responses, follow-up questioning, and resulting science explanations.

finding.finding_summary: In a sample of 63 French middle-school students (ages 14–15), task performance with unrestricted ChatGPT access remained only moderate despite all tasks being solvable with effective prompting. Mean success rate across six science problems was M=0.51 (SD=0.25), and students performed at chance in discriminating efficient from inefficient prompts (t=1.77, p=0.08) and useful from uninformative AI answers (Md′=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65), indicating weak support for conceptual understanding via spontaneous LLM use.
finding.measure: Binary-coded quality of students' final science explanations across six investigation tasks; prompt discrimination sensitivity (d'); AI answer evaluation sensitivity (d')
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.25 for success rate; SDd′=0.8 for prompt sensitivity; SDd′=1.2 for answer-evaluation sensitivity

finding.finding_summary: Students showed limited persistence/regulation in AI-mediated inquiry: only 14 of 63 students asked any follow-up questions, totaling 22 follow-up questions across all six tasks. Even when students recognized an answer as unsatisfactory, they initiated follow-up questions only 31.8% of the time, suggesting premature termination of inquiry and low sustained engagement in repairing understanding.
finding.measure: Behavioral regulation during inquiry, including frequency of follow-up questions after AI responses and premature termination of QA cycles

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial weaknesses in metacognitively regulated use of ChatGPT: students could not reliably distinguish efficient from inefficient prompts (mean d′=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08) or informative from low-level AI answers (mean d′=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65). Positive AI attitudes predicted worse prompt-quality sensitivity (β=-.39, p=.015) and worse answer-evaluation sensitivity (β=-.30, p=.018), while higher metacognitive regulation correlated with better prompt discrimination (r=.30, p=.022).
finding.measure: Prompt-quality discrimination, AI-answer evaluation sensitivity, follow-up regulation behavior, metacognitive and AI-attitude correlates
